extracted.intended_audience: administrative-law practitioners, agency lawyers, judges, regulated parties, and scholars studying judicial review and agency deference
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and doctrinal criteria for how courts should review and interpret agency actions and statutory questions (relation between Chevron deference, the APA, and older precedents). Useful for litigating or analyzing challenges to agency rules and interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article III judicial role: courts decide what the law is
rubrics_metrics.description: Article III assigns to the Federal Judiciary the responsibility and power to adjudicate 'Cases' and 'Controversies' and to interpret the laws; the final 'interpretation of the laws' is 'the proper and peculiar province of the courts.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts are to exercise independent judgment and interpretation (citing Marbury v. Madison and other early authorities). This underlies the presumption that questions of statutory interpretation are for courts to resolve, not for agencies to bind courts by their views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial independence from Executive interpretations
rubrics_metrics.description: While Executive Branch interpretations may inform courts, 'a judge certainly would not be bound to adopt the construction given by the head of a department.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Executive interpretations merit respect but do not supplant judicial judgment. Courts may consider agency views but retain final interpretive authority (citing Decatur, Burnet, and related precedents).

rubrics_metrics.name: APA §706 — courts decide legal questions and set aside unlawful agency action
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 5 U.S.C. §706, 'the reviewing court shall decide all relevant questions of law, interpret constitutional and statutory provisions, and determine the meaning or applicability of the terms of an agency action' and must 'hold unlawful and set aside agency action, findings, and conclusions found to be . . . not in accordance with law.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 706 codifies that courts, not agencies, resolve legal questions on review. It supplies the statutory basis for rejecting agency actions inconsistent with the law as the court interprets it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory standards of judicial review under the APA (arbitrary/capricious; substantial evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: The APA mandates deferential review for certain agency decisionmaking: agencies' policymaking and rulemaking can be set aside if 'arbitrary, capricious, [or] an abuse of discretion' (§706(2)(A)), and agency factfinding in formal proceedings is subject to the 'substantial evidence' standard (§706(2)(E)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While courts independently decide legal questions, they give deferential standards of review to agency policymaking (arbitrary/capricious) and to formal-adjudication factfinding (substantial evidence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Skidmore weight factors for agency interpretations
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency 'interpretations and opinions ... constitute[d] a body of experience and informed judgment to which courts and litigants [could] properly resort for guidance.' The weight of such a judgment 'depend[s] upon the thoroughness evident in its consideration, the validity of its reasoning, its consistency with earlier and later pronouncements, and all those factors which give it power to persuade, if lacking power to control.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even absent binding deference, courts may consider and give persuasive weight to agency interpretations assessed by these factors (thoroughness, reasoning, consistency, persuasive power).

rubrics_metrics.name: Chevron two-step framework (when applied)
rubrics_metrics.description: Chevron directs courts first to ask whether Congress has 'directly spoken to the precise question at issue'—if yes, that ends the matter. If Congress has not directly addressed the precise question (statute is 'silent or ambiguous'), the court asks whether the agency's interpretation is a 'permissible construction of the statute' and, if so, defers to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chevron's step one uses traditional statutory-construction tools to discern congressional intent; step two allows courts to defer when the statute is ambiguous and the agency's interpretation is permissible, justified by factors like regulatory complexity, agency expertise, policy formulation, and reasoned consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on Chevron-style deference — when deference is inappropriate or cabined
rubrics_metrics.description: Deferential review of agency legal interpretations is confined in certain contexts: courts historically refused to defer on pure legal questions and did not extend broad deference to all agency interpretations; deference was cabined to fact-bound determinations or cases where Congress 'specifically' delegated the authority to make the determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases like Gray v. Powell and Hearst show deference where Congress expressly left a determination to an agency or where an interpretive question was intertwined with agency factfinding; for pure statutory interpretation questions, courts retain primary responsibility and will not defer.

rubrics_metrics.name: When agency factual determinations are binding
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency determinations of fact are binding on courts 'provided that there was
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency factual findings are binding so long as there is evidence to support them and due process requirements (fair hearing, acting on evidence, not arbitrarily) are met (citing St. Joseph Stock Yards, Gray, Hearst). In formal adjudications, review uses the substantial-evidence standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contemporaneous and long-standing Executive construction as persuasive evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'contemporaneous construction of those who were called upon to act under the law ... is entitled to very great respect' and 'the long-standing
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contemporaneous construction by those who implement the law and long-standing practice can strongly inform a court’s determination of statutory meaning; such constructions can be especially useful when consistent over time (citing Edwards’ Lessee; Alabama Great Southern; National Lead; NLRB v. Noel Canning).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity is not an automatic delegation of interpretive power
rubrics_metrics.description: An ambiguity is not itself a delegation of law-interpreting power to an agency; Chevron 'confuses the two.' Ambiguities may be unintentional or result from Congress's inability to address every possible question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should not presume that every statutory ambiguity signals congressional intent to delegate interpretive authority to an agency. Courts must still use interpretive tools to discern the statute's best reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court's role in identifying and policing delegations of discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: When the best reading of a statute is that it delegates discretionary authority to an agency, the reviewing court must independently interpret the statute, 'fix the boundaries of [the] delegated authority,' and ensure the agency has engaged in 'reasoned decisionmaking' within those boundaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts determine whether a statute delegates decisionmaking authority and then enforce limits on that delegation (citing H. Monaghan; Michigan v. EPA; Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Assn. v. State Farm).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of statutory language that indicate congressional delegation
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress sometimes 'expressly delegate[s]' to an agency the authority to give meaning to particular statutory terms or to 'fill up the details' of a statutory scheme (examples include 29 U.S.C. §213(a)(15) and 42 U.S.C. §5846(a)(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit statutory language giving agencies authority to define terms or promulgate regulations signals that courts should treat agency interpretations as operating within an authorized delegation; even then, courts police that delegation for reasoned decisionmaking.
